'''Herbert Frank York''' (24 November 1921 &ndash; 19 May 2009) was an American [[nuclear physicist]] of [[Mohawk people|Mohawk]] origin. He held numerous research and administrative positions at various United States government and educational institutes.

==Biography==

Herbert York was born to a family of [[Mohawk nation|Mohawk]]<ref name=mohawk>{{cite web|url=https://www.edge.org/conversation/nsa-the-decision-problem|title=The Decision Problem|last=Dyson|first=George|date=2013-07-27|authorlink=George Dyson (science historian)|publisher=[[Edge.org|Edge]]}}</ref> ancestry, in [[Rochester, New York]]. He received his [[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]] and [[Master of Science|M.S.]] degrees from the [[University of Rochester]] in 1943,<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://physicstoday.scitation.org/do/10.1063/PT.4.2061/full/|title=Obituary of Herbert Frank York|journal=[[Physics Today]]|date=2009-05-21|issue=5 |doi=10.1063/PT.4.2061|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and then went on to obtain his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in 1949.<ref>{{cite web | author= | title=Biographies: Herbert York (b. 1921 d. May 19, 2009) | url=https://www.atomicarchive.com/Bios/York.shtml | work=The Atomic Archive | publisher=National Science Digital Library | year=2008 | accessdate=2008-11-30}}</ref> His dissertation advisor was future [[Nobel laureate]] [[Emilio Segrè]], and [[Robert Oppenheimer]] taught York's [[quantum mechanics]] class.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Manhattan Project: People > Scientists > HERBERT YORK |url=https://www.osti.gov/opennet/manhattan-project-history/People/Scientists/herbert-york.html |access-date=2024-02-21 |website=www.osti.gov}}</ref> During [[World War II]], he was a physicist at the [[Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory|Berkeley Radiation Laboratory]] and at [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]], working alongside [[Frank Oppenheimer]] as part of the [[Manhattan Project]]. After a brief stint as an [[assistant professor]] of physics at his doctoral alma mater in 1951, he was selected by [[Ernest Lawrence]] to serve as the inaugural director of the [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory|University of California Radiation Laboratory, Livermore Branch]] (1952&ndash;1958). 

Upon leaving Livermore, he held important positions in government for the remainder of the [[Eisenhower administration]], becoming the first chief scientist of the [[Advanced Research Projects Agency]] and the first [[director of Defense Research and Engineering]]. During this period, he "gradually became concerned that the United States and the Soviet Union were developing more weapons yet becoming less secure and that the shortened response times to a pre-emptive nuclear strike would put nuclear decision making in the hands of low-level military officers or, ultimately, computers," according to [[William J. Broad]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'', prompting his lifelong advocacy as a member of the [[anti-nuclear movement]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Grimes |first=William |date=2009-05-24 |title=Herbert York, 87, Top Nuclear Physicist Who Was Arms Control Advocate, Dies |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/05/25/us/25york.html |access-date=2024-02-21 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

He was the founding chancellor of the [[University of California, San Diego]] (1961&ndash;1964), where he remained on the physics faculty for the rest of his career, later serving as the institution's acting chancellor (1970&ndash;1972) amid the search for [[William J. McGill]]'s successor. An advisor to the [[Arms Control and Disarmament Agency]] in the 1960s, he returned to government service in earnest as the U.S. delegate to the [[CTBT|Comprehensive Test Ban]] negotiations in [[Geneva]], [[Switzerland]] (1979&ndash;1981); as part of this role, he was the chief U.S. negotiator in the unsuccessful effort to impose a comprehensive U.S.-Soviet nuclear test ban.<ref name=tiersten>{{Cite web | last = Tiersten | first = Sylvia | title = Herbert F. York, UC San Diego's first Chancellor. | url = http://alumni.ucsd.edu/magazine/vol6no1/features/feat2.htm | publisher = University of California, San Diego | date = January 2009 | access-date = 2009-05-25 | archive-date = 2009-02-18 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090218234319/http://alumni.ucsd.edu/magazine/vol6no1/features/feat2.htm | url-status = dead }}</ref>

York was director emeritus of the [[Institute on Global Conflict and Cooperation]] at UC San Diego and served as chairman of the university's Scientific and Academic Advisory Committee, which oversees activities at both Livermore and [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos National Laboratories]]. He also served on the board of the [[Council for a Livable World]], a nonpartisan [[arms control]] organization in Washington, D.C. York occasionally guest lectured for UC San Diego and other institutions.

York died 19 May 2009 in San Diego at age 87.<ref name=grimes>{{Cite news |last=Grimes |first=William |title=Herbert York, 87, Top Nuclear Physicist Who Was Arms Control Advocate, Dies  | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=May 25, 2009 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/05/25/us/25york.html?_r=1&hpw }}</ref>

==Publications==
*''Race to Oblivion'' (Simon & Schuster, 1970)<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.learnworld.com/ZNW/LWText.York.Race.Access.html|title=Race to Oblivion: A Participant's View of the Arms Race|year=1970|via=LearnWorld|last=York|first=Herbert F.|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220410112532/http://www.learnworld.com/ZNW/LWText.York.Race.Access.html |archive-date=2022-04-10 }}</ref>
*''Arms Control'' (Readings from Scientific American) (W.H. Freeman, 1973)
*''The Advisors: Oppenheimer, Teller and the Superbomb'' (W.H. Freeman, 1976), a book that [[Hans Bethe]] regarded as containing a highly accurate treatment of the "Russian H-bomb" test of 1953.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://permalink.lanl.gov/object/tr?what=info:lanl-repo/lareport/LA-UR-82-5215|title=Comments on The History of the H-Bomb|last=Bethe|first=Hans A.|journal=Los Alamos Science|date=Fall 1982|page=53}}</ref>
*''Race to Oblivion'' (Simon & Schuster, 1978)<ref>{{cite web |last=York|first=Herbert |title=Race to Oblivion: A Participant's View of the Arms Race |url=http://www.learnworld.com/ZNW/LWText.York.RaceToOblivion.html |publisher=Simon and Schuster |year=1978 |accessdate=2008-10-23 |archive-date=2015-10-31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151031012138/http://www.learnworld.com/ZNW/LWText.York.RaceToOblivion.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>
*''Making Weapons, Talking Peace: A Physicist's Journey from Hiroshima to Geneva'' (Harper & Row, 1987)
*''A Shield in Space? Technology, Politics and the Strategic Defense Initiative'' (U.C. Press, 1988, with Sanford Lakoff)
*''Arms and the Physicist'' (American Physical Society, 1994)
